title: Dynamic Programming: A Practical Guide to Solving Complex Problems

children.text: Dynamic programming
tackles complex problems by breaking them into simpler subproblems. This guide covers the core principles and the different approaches you'll actually use.
The focus here is practical: dynamic programming in Python, and how to actually optimize a solution instead of just describing it.
Fundamentals of Dynamic Programming
Definition and Core Principles

Dynamic programming solves problems that break down into simpler, overlapping subproblems. It's especially useful when the same subproblem shows up more than once, since you can reuse a result instead of recomputing it. That's really the whole idea: keep the solutions you already found, and skip the redundant work.
Problem Characteristics Suitable for Dynamic Programming

Two properties make a problem a good fit: optimal substructure, where the optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, where the same subproblem gets solved more than once. Fibonacci, the knapsack problem, and longest common subsequence are the classic examples. Both properties are what let dynamic programming cut
time complexity
compared to a naive recursive approach.
Overlapping Subproblems and Optimal Substructure

These two concepts are worth separating clearly. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblem gets solved repeatedly while working toward the larger solution, which is the whole reason dynamic programming is efficient. Optimal substructure means you can build the optimal solution from the optimal solutions of the subproblems. Get comfortable with both, and applying dynamic programming in Python starts to feel a lot less like magic.
Approaches to Dynamic Programming Algorithms

There are two main approaches, each with its own trade-offs: top-down, known as memoization, and bottom-up, known as tabulation. Knowing when to reach for each one matters more than memorizing the definitions.
Top-Down Approach (Memoization)

Top-down is recursive: you start at the main problem and break it down into smaller ones, caching each result the first time you compute it so you never redo the work. It's intuitive because it mirrors how you'd naturally think through the recursion, and in Python, decorators or a plain hash map are usually enough to implement it.
Bottom-Up Approach (Tabulation)

Bottom-up flips it around: solve the smallest subproblems first and iteratively build up to the final answer, with no recursion involved. You store results in a table or array, which avoids function call overhead and guarantees every subproblem is computed exactly once. In Python, a plain list with straightforward indexing is usually all you need.
Comparison Between Top-Down and Bottom-Up

Top-down tends to be more intuitive if you're newer to this, since it follows the recursion you'd already be thinking in. Bottom-up usually wins on space and time complexity, since a table avoids all the function call overhead. Both work fine in Python. Which one to use just depends on the problem in front of you.
Dynamic Programming in Python
Python makes both approaches easy to implement, mostly because of a couple of language features worth knowing well. Here's how that plays out in practice.
Implementing Memoization with Python Decorators
Python decorators make memoization pretty clean to implement. Here's the general shape of it:
Define a function that will compose the decorator.
Use a dictionary to store previously computed results.
Check the dictionary for a stored result before executing the function.
This keeps the code readable while still speeding things up. In practice, you can skip writing this by hand and just use the built-in functools.lru_cache for automatic memoization.
Building Bottom-Up Solutions Using Python Lists and Arrays
For bottom-up, you solve subproblems iteratively starting from the simplest, storing intermediate results in a Python list or array. The steps usually look like:
Defining the problem clearly and initializing the list to hold computed values.
Iteratively filling the list based on previously computed entries.
Returning the final result from the last entry in the list.
Every subproblem gets solved exactly once this way, which is where the time complexity savings come from.
Optimizing Space and Time Complexity in Python
There's usually a trade-off between time and space complexity, and Python gives you a couple of ways to tune both:
Using only the necessary state information to reduce memory usage instead of holding full arrays.
Implementing rolling arrays for problems that only need the results of the last few iterations.
Looking closely at what the problem actually requires usually reveals which variables you can drop or compress, which is where the real efficiency gains come from.
Common Pythonic Patterns in Dynamic Programming
A few patterns come up again and again when implementing dynamic programming in Python:
Recursive with memoization for clarity and straightforward implementation.
Iterative tabulation for better space optimization.
State compression to minimize memory usage while maintaining performance.
Recognizing these patterns early saves a lot of time once you are actually solving new problems.
Example: Longest Increasing Subsequence in Python
Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) is the classic example everyone uses to learn this. Here's the outline:
Initialize an array to store the lengths of the longest increasing subsequences found.
Iterate through each element, comparing it to all previous elements to identify potential subsequences.
Update the lengths based on comparisons, ultimately leading to the largest found value.
This runs in O(n²), though you can push it down further with binary search if you need the extra speed.
Fibonacci from naive recursion to constant memory

Fibonacci is the example I use to show what really changes when you apply dynamic programming, because the same problem goes through four versions with very different costs. The definition is F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) for n greater than 1.
The direct recursive version copies the definition as is. It works, but it recomputes the same values over and over: F(35) takes millions of calls.
This version runs in O(2^n) time and uses O(n) memory for the depth of the call stack.
With memoization I store each result the first time I compute it and return it directly after that. The code barely changes and the time drops to O(n).
With tabulation I build the solution bottom-up in an array, with no recursion. It stays at O(n) time and O(n) memory, but it no longer depends on the stack, so it won't blow up for large values of n.
The last step is noticing that each value only depends on the previous two. If I keep those two and drop the rest, memory falls to O(1).
That same reasoning, looking at which earlier states each cell depends on, is what I apply to any dynamic programming problem to cut memory.
The 0/1 knapsack in code

The 0/1 knapsack has a maximum capacity W and a list of n items, each with a weight and a value. Each item goes in whole or not at all, hence 0/1, and the goal is to maximize total value without exceeding the capacity.

The table dp[i][w] holds the best value you can get using the first i items with capacity w. The recurrence compares two options: leave item i out, which gives dp[i-1][w], or put it in if it fits, which gives its value plus dp[i-1][w - weight_i].

It runs in O(n·W) time and memory. Since each row only uses the previous one, you can keep a single row and drop memory to O(W), iterating w from high to low so you don't overwrite values you still need.
How I design a dynamic programming solution
When a problem smells like dynamic programming I always follow the same steps:
I define the state: which parameters describe a subproblem. In the knapsack, that's the item index and the remaining capacity.
I write the recurrence, the relation that says how a state's solution comes from smaller states. In optimal control this relation is known as the Bellman equation.
I set the base cases, the states I know without computing anything.
I pick the computation order: recursive with memoization if the problem is easier to think about top-down, a table if I want control over memory and to avoid the stack.
I check which states each cell depends on to see how much memory I can cut.
If I can't write step 2 clearly, the problem usually lacks optimal substructure and another technique fits better, like a greedy algorithm or backtracking.
Other problems where it shows up
Beyond the classics above, dynamic programming sits behind algorithms I use as references:
Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths from a node even with negative edge weights, and it detects negative cycles. Dijkstra doesn't work in that case because it's greedy.
Matrix chain multiplication finds the multiplication order that minimizes scalar operations by splitting the problem into subchains.
Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman align DNA or protein sequences, the first globally and the second locally, with a table very similar to the edit distance one.
Practicing on LeetCode
These three problems are the ones I'd start with if you're practicing for interviews, because each one forces a different part of the design process:
Climbing Stairs: counting the distinct ways to climb a staircase is Fibonacci in disguise, and it's a good place to practice going from recursion to constant memory.
Coin Change: the minimum number of coins for an amount is a clean tabulation exercise where the state is the remaining amount.
Edit Distance: the minimum operations to turn one string into another trains you to think in a two-dimensional table.
Memoization or tabulation in practice

Memoization only computes the subproblems the recursion needs, and it's usually quicker to write if the problem is already recursive. Its risk is stack depth: Python's default limit is around a thousand calls.
Tabulation computes every subproblem in order, even ones you don't need, but it doesn't use the stack and makes it more obvious where to cut memory.
My rule of thumb is to start with memoization to validate the recurrence and switch to a table once input size or memory starts to matter.
